claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning approach that accounts for oxygen and real defect states will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than conventional analytical models.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Conventional analytical models for HfNbTaTiZr assume a perfect, defect-free crystal lattice.
An as-cast bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen is representative of real-world impurity levels.
The proposed model combines defect-sensitive machine learning, ab initio simulations, and existing temperature-dependent transport measurements.
Temperature-dependent conductivity measurements are available for both nominally ideal and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen defect sites modify electron–phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen defect sites modify phonon transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Including compositional, defect, and microstructural features will better represent scattering and transport pathways than an ideal-lattice model.
Ideal-lattice assumptions introduce systematic conductivity-prediction errors for oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will reduce prediction errors by approximately 15–25% relative to standard analytical methods that neglect defects.
Existing defect-free analytical models overestimate the conductivity of oxygen-bearing HfNbTaTiZr by about 20% or more at both cryogenic and elevated temperatures.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 2 wt.% oxygen over about 0–1200 K.
Extrapolation beyond 1–2 wt.% oxygen or outside 0–1200 K is uncertain because calibration data are limited.
The held-out benchmark will use a near-1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr sample processed differently from the training specimens and measured over 5–150 K and 350–1000 K.
Deviation of measured conductivity from model predictions by more than 25% over more than half of the tested temperature range is the stated falsification threshold.
